assessmentSummary.identity: Arch Body Hold is an isometric prone long-body shape: lie face down with arms overhead and legs together, set a long whole-body line, then lift the chest, arms, and legs together only to a controllable height while the abdomen/pelvis remain supported. One bout ends with a deliberate lowering and reset. It is not a prone trunk-only extension, a leg-only lift, a dynamic superman repetition, a hollow-to-arch transition, a bridge, a rolling drill, a loaded back extension, or a diagnostic test.
currentCardFindings: Source 70 supplies only a generic name and a vague description; its empty taxonomy, anatomy, load, fatigue, environment, population, support, relationship, evidence, and media fields cannot be made selectable safely.

Combined upper- and lower-extremity prone lifting changes the mechanical task from isolated arm, leg, or trunk lifts. Lumbopelvic strategy and accumulated time under tension materially affect the task, so height and duration are controlled delivery variables, not a universal prescription.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Lie prone on a clean stable mat or floor with arms extended overhead and legs together. Establish a long whole-body line, then lift the chest, arms, and legs together only to a controllable height while the abdomen and pelvis remain supported. Breathe steadily, hold only while the line remains controlled, then lower deliberately and reset. Record exact limb position, hold duration, lift height, surface, symptoms, first quality loss, and rest. Trunk-only, arms-only, legs-only, dynamic, hollow-to-arch, rolling, bridge, loaded-extension, assessment, and other changed tasks require their own reviewed variant or definition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Lumbar Multifidus Muscle Thickness During Graded Quadruped and Prone Exercises
claims: The study distinguished prone upper-extremity, lower-extremity, and combined upper-and-lower-extremity lifts.
This candidate is the simultaneous combined-limb prone long-body hold only; partial-limb and dynamic tasks remain separate.

evidence.sourceTitle: Lumbar Multifidus Muscle Thickness During Graded Quadruped and Prone Exercises
claims: Combined upper-and-lower prone lifting is mechanically distinguishable from upper-only and lower-only lift conditions.
Arm position, leg position, support, lift height, and hold duration are explicit task dimensions rather than participant labels.

evidence.sourceTitle: Applying an active lumbopelvic control strategy during lumbar extension exercises: Effect on muscle recruitment patterns of the lumbopelvic region
claims: Prone extension tasks involve posterior trunk and hip-extensor recruitment patterns that change with lumbopelvic strategy.
The card records trunk, hip, shoulder, knee, and ankle task roles without making diagnosis, isolated-activation, prevention, or treatment claims.

evidence.sourceTitle: Applying an active lumbopelvic control strategy during lumbar extension exercises: Effect on muscle recruitment patterns of the lumbopelvic region
claims: Active lumbopelvic control changed lordosis and posterior-chain recruitment during prone extension exercises.
The candidate therefore requires a long controlled shape and modest controllable lift rather than a demand for maximal height or lumbar compression.

evidence.sourceTitle: Lumbar Multifidus Muscle Thickness During Graded Quadruped and Prone Exercises
claims: Combined prone arm-and-leg lifting is a distinct exercise condition from partial lifts.
Candidate scores describe task complexity and physical demand only, never participant proficiency, age, or classification.

evidence.sourceTitle: Derecruitment of the lumbar musculature with fatiguing trunk extension exercise
claims: Fatiguing trunk-extension exercise changed lumbar and hip-extensor recruitment patterns.
Track bout duration, lift height, line quality, surface, symptoms, and overlapping trunk or hip-extension work instead of asserting a universal recovery interval.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Instruction, supervision, setting, and progressive exposure are relevant safeguards for supervised exercise.
Use a clean stable floor or mat, clear prone station and exit, communication, and an exact task check; the card does not classify people.

evidence.sourceTitle: Derecruitment of the lumbar musculature with fatiguing trunk extension exercise
claims: Exercise duration and fatigue can affect posterior-chain recruitment patterns.
Candidate duration is quality-limited and review-only; the research does not establish a universal hold, set, frequency, or recovery prescription.

evidence.sourceTitle: Applying an active lumbopelvic control strategy during lumbar extension exercises: Effect on muscle recruitment patterns of the lumbopelvic region
claims: Lumbopelvic strategy affects prone extension mechanics.
Instructions explicitly set the prone base, overhead arms, together legs, simultaneous modest lift, breathing, controlled lower, and reset without demanding a diagnostic posture.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Appropriate instruction, supervision, environment, and progression are safeguards.
Stop for sharp or increasing pain, new neurologic/circulation/breathing/dizziness symptoms, inability to restore the long-body line, unsafe station, or participant request.

evidence.sourceTitle: Derecruitment of the lumbar musculature with fatiguing trunk extension exercise
claims: Trunk-extension recruitment patterns change as fatigue accumulates.
Use the exact low-impact candidate only when current fatigue, symptoms, logistics, duration, and downstream work fit; it does not promise transfer, prevention, or treatment.

claims: The study's graded exercise conditions support showing which limbs move in the exact candidate.
Athlete support must show base, whole-body line, modest simultaneous lift, breathing, controlled lower, self-check, and stop prompt in plain language.

evidence.sourceTitle: Applying an active lumbopelvic control strategy during lumbar extension exercises: Effect on muscle recruitment patterns of the lumbopelvic region
claims: Lumbopelvic control changes exercise mechanics and recruitment patterns.
Coaches should observe exact limb position, lift height, head/neck position, loss of line, breath-holding, duration, symptoms, and first quality loss without diagnosing a spinal condition.

claims: Instruction and supervision must be matched to task and setting.
